newsitem.title: USA: NBA BASKETBALL-JORDAN THE CHAMPIONSHIP DIFFERENCE AS USUAL.
newsitem.headline: NBA BASKETBALL-JORDAN THE CHAMPIONSHIP DIFFERENCE AS USUAL.

text.p: Michael Jordan was the difference again -- the NBA's man of the decade.

Jordan led the Chicago Bulls to their fifth championship in seven years -- and the fifth successive year he has played a full season -- when the defending champions beat the Utah Jazz 90-86 on Friday to wrap up the NBA Finals, four games to two.

Steve Kerr hit the game-winner, and Jordan was on the bench earlier in the fourth quarter when four bench men and his "little brother" in superstardom, swingman Scottie Pippen, forged a 10-0 streak to claw back into the game.
But it was Jordan who made the pass to Kerr for the biggest shot of his life, and it was Jordan who was the high scorer for the final quarter with 10 points.
Jordan, who averaged 32.3 points a game in the series, was the high scorer in all four Chicago wins, while Utah's Karl Malone was the high scorer in Utah's two victories.
Jordan's numbers in wins:

Game 1: 31 points, four rebounds, eight assists, and the buzzer-beating game-winner. Game 2: 38 points, 13 rebounds, nine assists, three steals. Game 5: 38 points, seven rebounds, five assists, three steals and a blocked shot. Game 6: 39 points, 11 rebounds, four assists, one steal, one blocked shot.
His numbers in losses:
Game 3: 26 points: 26 points, three rebounds, six assists, one steal, three blocks. Game 4: 22 points, four rebounds, four assists, no steals, no blocked shots.
For all their praise for Utah as their toughest opponent in five Finals, the Bulls' greatness as a team remained debatable.
First and most obviously, the two seasons Jordan spent time away playing baseball, the Bulls did not make the Finals.

The win tied coach Phil Jackson for second most titles with the Minneapolis Lakers' John Kundla behind the Boston Celtics' legendary Red Auerbach, who had eight, but that may just be an indication of a league now watered down with expansion clubs and stocked with overpaid, complacent players.
The Bulls were able to beat Utah even though Pippen, six-time rebounding champion Dennis Rodman and former Sixth Man of the Year Toni Kukoc were all playing their ways out of injury.
And the Jazz sputtered down the stretch of three games they could have won, taking only one close game.
"That really eats at you," said Jeff Hornacek. "With a turn here or there, it's us winning, not them."

Malone will long remember his two fatal missed free throws in Game 1, which allowed Jordan's buzzer-beater to win the game, his failure in Game 5 to block out Kukoc in the free throw lane, which led to to the nine-time scoring champion's back-breaker 3-pointer, his poor free throw shooting in Game 6.

Point guard John Stockton -- whose 127 playoff games without a championship put him in second place all-time behind Elgin Baylor (134) -- said Utah had learned a lot from the Bulls in their losses in Games 1 and 2.
For a team as veteran and accomplished as the Jazz, it was a somewhat strange admission.
But it was the first appearance in the Finals for the Jazz, who play out of the NBA's smallest city -- Salt Lake City, population 1.2 million.
The Bulls have faced five different opponents in their five Finals -- no Celtics versus Lakers matchup here.
Such a defining rivalry could occur only if Chicago and Utah -- the two conference winners, the one-two teams in won-lost records and scoring -- return.
"They really gave us a run and I look forward to seeing them here again," said Pippen.
"I don't have any doubt in my mind that we will get back here next year," said Utah centre Greg Ostertag.
Jordan tried to share the glory of his fifth Finals Most Valuable Player award with defensive stand-out Pippen. "We're a tandem," he said.

But in the end it was Jordan's buzzer-beater in Game 1, his Game 5 heroics after a night and day of nausea and fatigue caused by a viral infection, and his leadership throughout the series that will be remembered.

Jordan, noting the worth of the franchise had multiplied about ten-fold to $150 million since he arrived, used the victory to campaign for the rehiring of Jackson, upon which he has made his own return dependent, and for the retention of Pippen and even the controversial Rodman.
"We're entitled to defend what we have until we lose it," said Jordan.
